memory_candidates.content: When merging results from several independent single-term FTS5 (or any BM25-based) sub-queries into one ranked list, do NOT sort by the raw per-query relevance score as the primary key -- those scores are not comparable across independent queries (a generic word that is the entirety of one short document's match can score more extreme than a genuinely on-topic multi-word hit). Sort by cross-query corroboration (how many distinct sub-queries surfaced that result) as the PRIMARY key instead, with the raw score only as a same-tier tiebreak. Verified empirically: for a real ~250-document corpus and a 100-word natural-language query, raw-score-primary sorting returned zero topically relevant items in the top 10 despite non-empty recall; corroboration-primary sorting surfaced the corpus's own canonical textbook at position 1 for the same query.

A recall-count field alone (e.g. total_matched) is not a reliable sparse-vs-rich signal once a query is decomposed into many independent single-term sub-queries merged by OR: a genuinely off-topic query can still post a large total-match count purely from coincidental single-term hits scattered across unrelated documents in a large corpus. Add a second, stricter count (e.g. corroborated_count: results matched by >=2 distinct sub-queries) and use IT for any sparse/confidence signal once the sub-query count is large, while leaving the raw total-match count and displayed results unchanged. This mirrors an existing >=2-distinct-hits asymmetry pattern for exactly this class of long, generic-word-heavy query.

Bash heredocs opened unquoted (<< PYEOF, not << 'PYEOF') perform command substitution INSIDE the heredoc body, including on backticks in prose/docstrings -- a Python docstring containing `identifier` inside such a heredoc silently triggers bash to try running `identifier` as a shell command (visible only as a stray stderr line like '<name>: command not found'), not a syntax error. When writing Python source inside an unquoted bash heredoc (needed for $variable substitution into the script), use single-quotes for any in-prose emphasis instead of backticks.
